The classification method serves as a foundational concept in machine learning, providing simplicity and interpretability. It allows for the straightforward categorization of inputs into predefined classes. Additionally, its computational efficiency makes it suitable for applications with limited resources. However, the classification method does have its limitations. It lacks fine-grained information, such as spatial details or the ability to handle multiple objects simultaneously. This makes it less suitable for tasks that require precise localization or the identification of multiple objects at once. On the other hand, object detection methods not only provide class labels but also offer precise spatial information, which addresses the challenge of localization. These methods excel in scenarios where multiple objects need to be handled and are versatile for tasks like instance segmentation and keypoint detection. Despite their advantages, object detection methods are more complex to implement. They require bounding box regression and labor-intensive data annotation. Moreover, they often demand significant computational resources, which restricts their deployment in real-time and resource-constrained environments. The choice between classification and object detection depends on the available data and the specific requirements of the task. CHALLENGES IN PLANT DISEASE DETECTION After a detailed review of ML and DL algorithms for plant disease detection and classification and the detailed computational study on five state-of-the-art object detection algorithms for plant disease detection and eighteen state-of-the-art classification algorithms for plant disease classification on a widely-used dataset, we have identified several challenges in practical applications of plant disease detection: 1) There is a lack of models that handle non-image data. Most existing classification and object detection algorithms focus solely on image data, neglecting other relevant information such as temperature and humidity. Developing techniques to incorporate non-image data is essential for more accurate predictions. 2) There are only a few completely annotated open datasets. Many studies rely on the PlantVillage dataset, which was obtained in a controlled laboratory setting. Generating larger datasets under real-world conditions is crucial. Collaborative efforts are needed to create representative datasets. 3) Most works treat the disease detection problem as a classification problem, either binary classification or multi-class classification. In addition, we perform an extensive computational study on five state-of-the-art object detection algorithms on the PlantDoc dataset to detect the diseases on the leaves, and eighteen state-of-the-art classification algorithms on the PlantDoc dataset, to predict whether or not there is a disease in a leaf and which one it is. For the object detection problem, YOLOv5 is able to achieve a high accuracy not only at the strict AP metric of the COCO challenge but also in the detection of small, medium, and large objects in the images. For the classification problem, the networks ResNet50 and MobileNetv2 had the most optimal trade-off on accuracy and training time. ResNet50 achieved a total accuracy of 61.01% and was trained on about 18 minutes, while MobileNetv2 achieved a total accuracy of 59.74% and was trained for about 16 minutes. In future work, we plan to study more algorithms for classification and object detection on more datasets to see whether the results are consistent across different datasets. We also intend to study some image preprocessing and data augmentation techniques to see whether the accuracy of the algorithms can be improved with these techniques. ABSTRACT Crop diseases remain a major threat to global agricultural productivity, particularly in resource-constrained regions, where early intervention is critical to ensuring food security. Smallholder farmers often practice intercropping, creating complex field conditions that challenge conventional disease detection systems. Although computer vision and machine learning offer powerful tools for early diagnosis, most existing approaches are tailored to single-crop scenarios and rely on cloud-based or high-resource environments, limiting their applicability in the field. This review synthesizes and explores recent advances in AI-based crop disease detection with emphasis on multi-crop and intercropped systems. We provide an overview of the detection pipeline from data acquisition and preprocessing to model training and deployment. CROP DISEASES Crops are affected by a wide range of diseases, each posing significant challenges to their health and productivity. Crops are susceptible to fungal, bacterial, viral, nematode and parasitic diseases [28]. These crop diseases can damage the entire yields prior to harvesting if not monitored, detected, managed and controlled promptly [4]. TRADITIONAL APPROACHES TO CROP DISEASE DETECTION Traditional crop disease detection relies on visual inspection, field surveys, and indigenous knowledge to identify visible symptoms such as leaf discoloration or shape deformation [29], [30]. Farmers and agricultural centers conduct surveys and sampling, often supported by extension workers who provide expert diagnosis and management advice. They also depend on traditional forecasting methods, using past seasonal patterns to anticipate outbreaks [31], [32], and monitor pest populations as early indicators of diseases [33], [34]. Environmental conditions such as rainfall, humidity, and high moisture levels are monitored by farmers, as they are closely associated with fungal infections [35], [36]. However, these approaches are time-consuming, error-prone, costly, and limited by the availability and expertise of professionals, making them unfavorable for large and resource-constrained farms [37].

DATA PREPROCESSING Effective data preprocessing is crucial in preparing datasets for machine learning-based crop disease detection. Raw datasets often contain inconsistencies such as blurred images, poor lighting, or distortions caused by different environmental conditions. Preprocessing improves image quality and consistency, improving the accuracy and reliability of trained models. The most common preprocessing techniques include image resizing and normalization to maintain consistent dimensions and pixel ranges, contrast enhancement to improve the visibility of disease symptoms, and noise reduction to remove artifacts or irrelevant features that may hinder model training [97], [137]. Data augmentation techniques such as rotation, flipping, and scaling which help increase dataset diversity and improve model robustness against variations in lighting, orientation, and image quality [138], [139]. Methods such as filtering, geometric transformations, and mathematical morphology are used to refine image structure before features are extracted. Feature learning is further improved using algorithms such as Principal Component Analysis (PCA) and autoencoders for dimensionality reduction and anomaly detection [48], [140]. Additionally, Gaussian Mixture Models (GMM) have been used to model underlying data distributions for unsupervised preprocessing tasks. Models trained on inadequately preprocessed images tend to exhibit lower predictive performance, particularly when deployed on mobile or edge devices that are more sensitive to lighting, shadow, and angle variations. Targeted segmentation enables more accurate feature extraction and contributes to higher model performance in classification tasks [141]. Several segmentation techniques have been explored for agricultural imagery, including deep learning methods such as U-Net and EfficientNet, encoder–decoder architectures, multi-scale approaches, dilated convolutional networks, visual attention models, generative adversarial networks (GANs), graph neural networks (GNNs), instance segmentation networks, and transformer-based models [142], [143]. U-Net hybrid models have demonstrated high segmentation accuracy, particularly in localizing leaf diseases [144]. Fully Convolutional Networks and Mask R-CNN are used to generate precise pixel-level masks for lesions [145]. Classical techniques of thresholding, region growing, K-means clustering, watershed algorithm, graph-based segmentation, and conditional random fields (CRF) offer simpler alternatives, especially when computational resources are limited [107]. In practice, segmentation pipelines often consist of multiple stages. For example, beginning with K-means clustering for initial segmentation, followed by gradient computation and region adjacency graph construction to refine boundaries. Segmentation quality is significantly affected by the choice of color space [146]. When effectively applied, segmentation techniques produce detailed, pixellevel classification masks that enable disease detection and classification, thereby improving overall performance of models [144]. MODEL TRAINING FOR CROP DISEASE DETECTION The training stage typically involves splitting datasets into training, validation, and test sets, followed by model selection, hyperparameter tuning, and iterative model training and validation. Some of the machine learning and deep learning algorithms commonly used include Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), Support Vector Machines (SVM), Decision Trees, Gradient Boosting methods (e.g., XGBoost), Naive Bayes, Long Short-Term Memory networks (LSTM), and Random Forests, among others [71], [151], [152]. CNNs have emerged as the dominant architecture for image-based crop disease detection because of their ability to learn spatial feature hierarchies from images [146], [153], [154]. Studies have shown CNNs to be effective in identifying visual disease symptoms such as leaf discoloration, spot distribution, lesion patterns, and shape anomalies [155]. CNNs can analyze complex crop features such as color variations, texture patterns, lesion shapes, and spatial arrangements of disease symptoms [41], [43], [156]. 217274

Model performance in crop disease detection is often constrained by small or imbalanced datasets. To overcome these limitations, transfer learning has been widely adopted, enabling the fine-tuning of pre-trained models such as ResNet, MobileNet, DenseNet, and EfficientNet [6], [157]. This strategy accelerates convergence, enhances generalization, and reduces training time, particularly in data-scarce or resource-constrained settings [158]. In parallel, custom architectures have been developed to address domain-specific challenges such as multi-disease or multi-crop recognition, where diverse symptom patterns demand tailored network designs. While deep learning architectures dominate image-based disease detection, classical machine learning algorithms including Support Vector Machines (SVM), Random Forests, K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), and Decision Trees remain relevant for structured or tabular data, such as spectral indices, environmental sensor readings, or low-resolution imagery. Moreover, ensemble methods like Gradient Boosting (e.g., XGBoost) have shown competitive performance in predicting early disease severity from handcrafted features [146]. Model selection is typically task-dependent and guided by computational constraints and deployment goals. Lightweight models such as MobileNet are favored for on-field edge applications, where efficiency and low power consumption are critical, whereas high-capacity architectures like EfficientNet are suited for centralized, computationrich environments. In complex agricultural settings, custom or hybrid networks are often proposed to handle multiple diseases or crop types simultaneously, achieving higher adaptability and robustness. EFFICIENT AI MODELS FOR EDGE DEPLOYMENT Recent research has focused on deploying lightweight machine learning models on edge devices to enable efficient, low-latency inference without relying on cloud connectivity. For example, MobileNet, a compact deep learning architecture, has been used for non-intrusive load monitoring on smartphones, with TensorFlow Lite further compressing the model to reduce memory usage and computation time [121], [162]. Studies have shown that models deployed at the edge can achieve faster response times than cloud-based systems while maintaining comparable accuracy, demonstrating the potential of edge AI for real-time and secure applications [163]. To address the strict resource constraints of embedded systems, researchers have explored lightweight CNNs, quantized and pruned architectures, and emerging edge-optimized transformers such as MobileViT, Tiny-ViT, and EdgeFormer. OPEN CHALLENGES AND RESEARCH OPPORTUNITIES Several limitations in previous studies, along with emerging trends and future research directions, have been identified. This section summarizes these insights, emphasizing the development of lightweight models suitable for deployment on embedded devices that operate under constrained computational and energy conditions [6]. A. CURRENT LIMITATIONS Although machine learning and computer vision have shown great promise for early crop disease detection, several limitations still hinder their practical deployment and effectiveness in real-world farming environments. 1) GENERALIZATION AND REGIONAL ADAPTABILITY Models trained on datasets from one geographical region may fail to generalize well in another region due to differences in soil type, climate, crop varieties and farming practices. An example is that a model trained on East African crop datasets may not perform as expected in West Africa due to differences in crop features and varieties [168], [169]. Models trained in controlled environments like lab settings may not perform as expected in real-world scenarios where these conditions are inconsistent because they lack robustness. Cloudbased models require stable internet access for inference and relevant infrastructure which is often unreliable in remote farming regions. For example, a mobile app requiring cloud-based inference might fail in offline mode. Real-time inference in such areas is unreliable and limited by poor internet connectivity making it critical to shift toward edge and offline inference capable architectures. VII. CONCLUSION Crop disease recognition using computer vision and machine learning presents potential solutions to the persistent challenges faced by smallholder farmers, especially in regions prone to food insecurity. Whereas numerous techniques and frameworks have been proposed, their practical application in real-world farming contexts particularly in intercropped and resource-constrained environments remains limited. This review has identified key challenges including dataset scarcity and lack of diversity, limited support for multi-crop detection, the absence of real-time offline capabilities, and high barriers to adoption due to infrastructure and usability issues. Moreover, most existing systems are designed for cloud-based environments and single crop scenarios, making them unsuitable for the heterogeneous, low-connectivity settings typical of many rural agricultural areas. Emerging opportunities such as lightweight models for edge deployment, multimodal data fusion, and the integration of AI with IoT and mobile tools offer a direction to bridge these gaps. In addition, conversational AI systems that use large language models have the potential to offer contextual and multilingual support that is directly accessible to farmers. text: Multi-Crop Plant Disease Detection using PlantDoc Akshaj Saini Computer Science & Engineering Chandigarh University Mohali, India akshajsaini846@gmail.com Swati Panwar Computer Science & Engineering Chandigarh University Mohali, India Swati.e16019@cumail.in Parteek Madaan Computer Science & Engineering Chandigarh University Mohali, India parteekmadaan45@gmail.com Sahil Kaushik Computer Science & Engineering Chandigarh University Mohali, India kaushik0112sahil@gmail.com Priyanka Kumari Computer Science & Engineering Chandigarh University Mohali, India kpbuxar39@gmail.com Abstract— We present a deep-learning approach for detecting diseases across multiple crop types using the PlantDoc dataset. Our method combines a classification network and an object detection network to identify both the disease category and the location of infected regions in an image. We first preprocess each image and feed it into a convolutional neural network (CNN) that outputs the most likely disease class. Simultaneously, a detection pipeline (e.g. a YOLO-based model) localizes diseased leaf areas with bounding boxes. We evaluate our approach on the PlantDoc dataset (which contains 13 plant species and 30 disease classes) and report performance in terms of accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, and mean Average Precision (mAP). Our experiments show that the proposed multi-crop model achieves high accuracy and robust localization across diverse plant types. These results suggest that our system can serve as a useful tool for scalable plant disease monitoring in real-world agricultural settings. Conventional diagnostics are weighed down by the inadequate infrastructure in laboratories and the need to depend on the expertise of clinicians, especially in rural and limited resources places [1]. The advent of computer vision and deep learning has led to scalable, non-invasive detectors applicable in the real-world agricultural setting [2]. To address the acute shortage of field based, large scale datasets, the PlantDoc dataset was proposed, consisting of some 2,600 annotated images of 13 plant species and up to 17 disease classes, generated with intensive annotation effort [1][3]. PlantDoc, in contrast to lab-only data, focuses on images taken in the field where the lighting conditions and the background are not controlled and will be more relevant to the in-field diagnostic problem [2][4]. It incorporates both the classification and object detection variants-encompassing bounding-box annotations of both diseased and healthy areas in a plant, allowing a localization as well as a recognition task [5][6]. It incorporates both the classification and object detection variants-encompassing bounding-box annotations of both diseased and healthy areas in a plant, allowing a localization as well as a recognition task [5][6]. With this richness, classification models (e.g., CNNs) and detection frameworks such as Faster R-CNN or MobileNet can be benchmarked and used to localize disease on leaves [7][8]. Despite all these encouraging advances, there are two additional critical concerns, including the imbalance of the dataset and the variance of class frequency associated, whereby only dozens of samples represent a particular class, and the comparison of classification-only and detectionbased protocols under multi-plant and multi-disease settings [13]. text: A. Dataset Preparation We use the data of the PlantDoc, 2,598 labelled pictures of 13 plant species and 17 disease or healthy conditions. To be classified, the data is transformed into image samples with class labels. To be detected, the bounding box annotations in the XML format (Pascal VOC) are stored to be used to train the detection models. The images are rescaled to 224X224, normalized and divided into 70 percent training, 15 percent validation and testing sets. Challenges There are a few important challenges in developing an efficient multi-crop plant disease detection system based on the PlantDoc data. First, there is a great problem of class imbalance- some diseases, e.g. tomato healthy and grape black rot are represented by very large numbers of samples, others e.g. jute disease and papaya ringspot have very few. This disproportion biases the learning and hurts recall and accuracy to minority classes. Second, disease symptoms (e.g., leaf blight vs. bacterial spots), especially when not given in their spatial context, can be confused because of the visual similarity of different symptoms. B. Limitations Although good outcomes were obtained in this research, there are a few limitations that need to be recognized. To begin with, the PlantDoc data is very small and skewed, particularly on some combinations of crop-disease. This restricts the generalizability of deep learning models to all disease classes, especially the ones that are under-represented. Both classification and detection models have much worse performance on rare diseases, potentially limiting their use in practice in a variety of agricultural environments. VII. This study presents inline-eq-IEq1PlantNet, a novel lightweight multi-class classification model based on a modified MobileNet architecture, designed to detect plant leaf diseases across a diverse range of crop types. inline-eq-IEq 2PlantNet employs depthwise separable convolutions to significantly reduce model complexity without compromising accuracy. The architecture integrates Batch Normalization (BN) and Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU) activation after each convolutional layer, while a multi-stage design enhances feature extraction and overall performance. MobileNet V1, though efficient, suffers from training instability, slower convergence, and reduced performance in deeper layers. These issues are largely due to the absence of BN and ReLU, resulting in internal covariate shifts and limited nonlinearity. By incorporating BN and ReLU after both depthwise and pointwise convolution layers, the proposed model stabilizes the training process, reduces covariate shift, and enables faster convergence. ReLU further introduces the non-linearity required for learning more complex patterns, all while maintaining computational efficiency. Additionally, the model retains the core structure of MobileNet with repeated MobileNet blocks, starting with depthwise convolution followed by BN and ReLU, and concluding with pointwise convolution, again followed by BN and ReLU. This design improves gradient flow, minimizing the risk of vanishing gradients and enhancing the model’s capacity to learn deeper features. The first block in each stage employs downsampling to reduce spatial dimensions, while subsequent blocks preserve them with a stride of 1, maintaining the model’s lightweight nature. These modifications not only resolve the limitations of MobileNet V1 but also ensure that the model remains efficient and suitable for mobile and embedded applications. Conclusion This paper presents inline-eq-IEq89PlantNet, a novel, lightweight CNN architecture designed for multi-class plant disease classification. The model achieved a high classification accuracy of 99%, along with impressive performance metrics such as precision, recall, F1 score, sensitivity, specificity, and MCC, while using only 389,286 parameters. To validate generalization and reduce dataset-specific bias, 5-fold cross-validation demonstrated stable performance, with an average accuracy of 97.96% and a standard deviation of 0.25%, highlighting robustness and consistency. INTRODUCTION Agriculture plays a pivotal role in bolstering a nation's economic growth, predominantly by increasing crop production. The early identification of plant diseases assumes an even more critical role in preserving global health [1]. Early detection facilitates timely intervention, mitigating the adverse effects that can be financially burdensome for farmers, entailing crop losses, increased pesticide consumption, and reduced yields. text: 210 V. CONCLUSION The study focused on YOLOv5, YOLOv7 and YOLOv8 models for citrus plant disease detection. YOLOv8s has achieved 96.1% mAP@50-95% for citrus disease detection and mAP@50-95% of 95.3%, 96.0% and 97.0% for detection of Anthracnose, Melanose and Bacterial Brown Spot diseases, respectively. The developed model for detection of citrus diseases can significantly help the farmers to identify the disease and locate the infected region, improve crop yield production, efficient usage of resources, reduce cost and environmental effects. The model will also enable the potential for applications of Precision Agriculture Technologies (PATs). The developed model is small and can be used for IoT devices e.g., precision agriculture technologies, however, larger models such as YOLOv8m, YOLOv8l and YOLOv8x can be custom trained for more datasets and complex scenarios. The model has better detection speed and accuracy in experimental results, but it needs to be further experimented for real-time detection in real-world scenarios. For future work, the developed model should be trained and validated on multiple datasets for different plant species disease detection. The developed model can be integrated with PATs e.g., an aerial high resolution imagery crop survey drone and custom developed application based on Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) for field location marking, to detect the plant diseases and locate the infected field areas which can be helpful to plan and execute pesticide spray activity, control the disease, and increase crop productivity. text: Page 34 of 43 CNNs are specifically designed for handling image data, as they can automatically learn hierarchical features from raw pixel values. They use convolutional layers to capture local patterns and hierarchical representations, enabling them to excel at tasks like object recognition, image detection, and classification. DL and ML both have roles in image detection and classification. ML techniques like SVMs may be sufficient for simple image detection and classification tasks with well-defined features. However, DL, including CNNs, is typically more powerful and versatile for complex image tasks. DL models can automatically learn intricate features and representations, reducing the need for manual feature engineering. Hence, for most modern image detection classification tasks, DL, particularly CNNs, is the preferred choice due to their ability to outperform traditional ML techniques in terms of accuracy and efficiency [161]. CNNs are often the favored choice for image detection and classification due to their inherent capacity to autonomously acquire pertinent image features and grasp spatial hierarchies. Nevertheless, the selection between conventional ML and DL hinges on the particular problem, the accessibility of data, and the computational capabilities accessible. In numerous advanced image detection and classification tasks, DL, mainly through CNNs, is preferred when ample data and computational resources are available. authors: Ameer Tamoor Khan; Signe Marie Jensen; Abdul Rehman Khan; Shuai Li

text: Plant disease detection model for edge computing devices Ameer Tamoor Khan 1, Signe Marie Jensen 1*, Abdul Rehman Khan 2 and Shuai Li 3 1Department of Plant and Environmental Science, University of Copenhagen, Copenhagen, Denmark, 2Department of Computer and Information Sciences, Pakistan Institute of Engineering and Applied Sciences, Islamabad, Pakistan, 3Deparment of Information Technology and Electrical Engineering, University of Oulu, Oulu, Finland In this paper, we address the question of achieving high accuracy in deep learning models for agricultural applications through edge computing devices while considering the associated resource constraints. Traditional and state-ofthe-art models have demonstrated good accuracy, but their practicality as enduser available solutions remains uncertain due to current resource limitations. One agricultural application for deep learning models is the detection and classiﬁcation of plant diseases through image-based crop monitoring. We used the publicly available PlantVillage dataset containing images of healthy and diseased leaves for 14 crop species and 6 groups of diseases as example data. The MobileNetV3-small model succeeds in classifying the leaves with a test accuracy of around 99.50%. Post-training optimization using quantization reduced the number of model parameters from approximately 1.5 million to 0.93 million while maintaining the accuracy of 99.50%. The ﬁnal model is in ONNX format, enabling deployment across various platforms, including mobile devices. These ﬁndings offer a cost-effective solution for deploying accurate deep-learning models in agricultural applications. While applying pesticides can prevent or limit the impact of most plant diseases, their use should be restricted due to environmental considerations. Early and efﬁcient detection of plant diseases and their distribution in the ﬁeld is crucial for effective treatment. The implementation of automatic plant disease detection systems is, therefore, essential for efﬁcient crop monitoring. Deep Learning Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and computer vision are two developing AI technologies that have recently been employed to identify plant leaf diseases automatically. Already in 1980, Fukushima (1980) presented a visual cortex-inspired multilayer artiﬁcial neural network for image classiﬁcation. The network showed that the initial layer detects simpler patterns with a narrow receptive ﬁeld, while later levels combine patterns from earlier layers to identify more complex patterns with wider ﬁelds. text: Krizhevsky et al. (2012) developed the AlexNet architecture, which helped them win the ImageNet Large Scale Visual Recognition Challenge. Several CNN (Convolutional Neural Network) designs have been introduced since then Krizhevsky et al. (2012); Fu et al. (2018); Yang et al. (2023); Dutta et al. (2016); Sarda et al. (2021). These models are called “deep learning” architectures due to their 5200 layers. Early investigations employed manually created characteristics from leaf picture samples. Later, the trends shifted to DCNN (Deep Convolutional Neural Network) architectures capable of effectively classifying data and automatically extracting features. Plant disease picture classiﬁcation has been used to test a variety of CNN architectures Amara et al. (2017); Sladojevic et al. (2016); Setiawan et al. (2021); Yang et al. (2023); Qiang et al. (2019); Swaminathan et al. (2021); Schuler et al. (2022). Plant disease diagnosis through image analysis employs various machine learning techniques Ferentinos (2018). These methods identify and classify diseases affecting cucumbers, bananas Fujita et al. (2016), cassavas Amara et al. (2017), tomatoes Ramcharan et al. (2017), and wheat Fuentes et al. (2017). Ramcharan et al. (2017) tested ﬁve architectures—AlexNet, AlexNetOWTBn, GoogLeNet, Overfeat, and VGG on 58 classes of healthy and sick plants. AlexNet achieved 99.06% and VGG 99.48% test accuracy. Despite the large variation in trainable parameters, these designs had test accuracy above 99%. Maeda-Gutiérrez et al. (2020) tested ﬁve architectures for tomato illnesses. All architectures tested had accuracies above 99%. However, when tested on ﬁeld pictures, Ramcharan et al. (2017) encountered shadowing and leaf misalignment.

MobileNetV3’s efﬁcient and compact design offers a strategic advantage in addressing the imbalances inherent in datasets like PlantVillage. By leveraging transfer learning, a pre-trained MobileNetV3 is later ﬁne-tuned on PlantVillage classes, harnessing generalized features to counteract dataset disparities. Its lightweight nature facilitates rapid training, enabling extensive data augmentation to enhance underrepresented classes. Furthermore, MobileNetV3 can serve as a potent feature extractor, with the derived features being suitable for synthetic sample generation techniques like SMOTE or ADASYN to achieve class balance. The model’s cost-effectiveness allows for swift iterative experiments, incorporating regularization techniques to deter overﬁtting dominant classes. Overall, MobileNetV3 presents a versatile toolset for researchers to navigate and mitigate the challenges of unbalanced datasets. Training MobileNetV3 on the PlantVillage dataset and applying it to new images introduces challenges related to generalization. Absent categories, like healthy orange and squash, might be misclassiﬁed into familiar classes the model has seen. Diseases not in the training data, such as brown spots on soybeans, could be wrongly identiﬁed as another visually similar ailment or even as a healthy state. The model might also grapple with new images that differ in lighting, resolution, or background, especially if not exposed to such variations during training. text: Plant Disease Detection Over Multiple Datasets Using AlexNet Palika Jajoo∗ Swami Keshvanand Institute of Technology Management & Gramothan, Jaipur, India palika@skit.ac.in Mayank Kumar Jain Manipal University, Jaipur, India mayank.jain@jaipur.manipal.edu Sarla Jangir Swami Keshvanand Institute of Technology Management & Gramothan, Jaipur, India sarlajangir11@gmail.com ABSTRACT Plants diseases are responsible for huge loss of crop yield. Manual inspection of plant disease is a time taken and inefficient process. Image processing and machine learning-based approaches have been offered as a solution for creating such automated plant disease detection systems. Plant diseases leads to change in color and texture of leave, this property is used for developing plant disease detection systems. Deep learning models such as Visual Geometry Group (VGG) and ResNET are extensively used in this field. However, most of these models are not scalable as they are either focused on disease classification on a particular crop or dataset. The focus of this study is to showcase a new method for identifying leaf diseases. AlexNet is used in the system’s development, and it is trained and verified using data from many sources. Results indicate improved performance as compared to previously published works. CCS CONCEPTS • Computing methodologies →Machine learning. When Gaussian noise is applied to a leaf picture, the vein boundaries become blurry, distorting the leaf’s overall appearance. The size, shape, and pattern of leaves are all altered by splash noise. These noise-free leaf photos must be restored using speckle and Gaussian noise reduction methods. Most plant disease detection techniques employed support vector machines, K-nearest neighbors, and spatial gray-level dependency matrices (SGDM). These techniques may be used to study both healthy and sick plant leaves. Kaur et al. [11] investigated neural networks and back-propagation algorithms for use in pattern recognition. While these procedures may be relied upon, they fall short of being seriously regarded for agricultural illnesses in the actual world. For their solution, the authors demonstrated a preprocessing method based on nature. Preprocessing techniques were employed to reduce noise. Padmavathi et al. [12] contrasted the efficacy of RGB and Gray scale pictures for disease detection in leaves. The hue of diseased leaves is an indicator of the level of infection. The severity of the illness was estimated using a combination of grayscale and color photographs, segmentation, and a median filter for image enhancement.

Workers needed to identify diseases and determine the type of lesions from a large number of plants. [13] introduced vision transformers, derived from the original Transformer architecture. The ViT consists of several stacked encoder blocks, each incorporating three modules within the ViT model: a multi-head attention (MHA) or self-attention, normalization layer (NORM), and an MLP layer [14]. The architecture of the ViT model is depicted in Figure 1. To input an image into the original vision transformers, it undergoes an initial division into non-overlapping patches of a fixed size. Subsequently, these overlapped patches are compressed and converted into representations with fewer dimensions. Every flattened patch undergoes a trainable linear transformation to generate its respective “positional encoding” along with “linear projection”. The resulting vector from these operations is fed through a sequence of N ViT transformer blocks [2]. Ultimately, the final output of ViT is directed into one or multiple fully connected layers, which are responsible for performing image classification. 3.3 Model for plant diseases detection using a hybrid ViT CNN approach The objectives of this study are to develop a hybrid model that integrates the capabilities of ViT and CNN for the identification and detection of plant diseases. To overcome this challenge, this study employs a convolutional layer to proficiently extract local features, thereby enhancing the model’s inductive bias for locality. The proposed hybrid model’s architectural representation is shown in Figure 2. All input images, initially with dimensions of 224×224×3, undergo a convolutional layer to extract local features. The feature map from this convolutional layer is then converted into patches, each with dimensions of 16×16. After flattening, these patches are linearly projected, producing a feature vector with dimensions of 196×768. Subsequently, these vectors pass through a stack of N transformer blocks intended to extract global features. The number of transformer blocks in this study is minimized to reduce the computational cost of the proposed model. For classification purposes, an MLP block is introduced, comprising a dense layer with Softmax activation. This layer contains neurons corresponding to number of categories in dataset.

The transfer learning method can transfer the knowledge learned from the general large dataset to the professional ﬁelds with relatively little data. But for the datasets with only a few or dozens of images, the transfer learning method also has the problem of low recognition accuracy [23]. This is because it is difﬁcult for the deep network to learn different features, which leads to problems that are difﬁcult to converge or over-ﬁtting. Therefore, plant disease datasets with single or small samples can hardly support the training of DL architecture. On the other hand, for the recognition of new classes that do not appear in the training set, the deep learning model needs to be retrained. Recent advances in DL have proven the effectiveness of several architectures to learn new classes using small datasets, a famous sub-ﬁeld known as Few-Shot Learning (FSL) [89]. FSL can not only solve the recognition problem of new classes that did not appear in the training but also solve the problem of the neural network, which difﬁcult to converge due to the small number of experimental samples, thereby improving the accuracy of small datasets recognition. The FSL methods used for image classiﬁcation include model initialization, metric learning and data generate methods. The initialization method focuses on the adjustable parameters in the network so that a new class of classiﬁer can be learned from a limited set of examples [90]–[92]. CONCLUSION AND FUTURE DIRECTIONS In this paper, we have introduced the basic knowledge of deep learning and presented a comprehensive review of recent research work done in plant leaf disease recognition using deep learning. Provided sufﬁcient data is available for training, deep learning techniques are capable of recognizing plant leaf diseases with high accuracy. The importance of collecting large datasets with high variability, data augmentation, transfer learning, and visualization of CNN activation maps in improving classiﬁcation accuracy, and the importance of small sample plant leaf disease detection and the importance of hyper-spectral imaging for early detection of plant disease have been discussed. At the same time, there are also some inadequacies. Most of the DL frameworks proposed in the literature have good detection effects on their datasets, but the effects are not good on other datasets,

Most of the DL frameworks proposed in the literature have good detection effects on their datasets, but the effects are not good on other datasets, that is the model has poor robustness. Therefore, better robustness DL models are needed to adapt the diverse disease datasets. In most of the researches, the PlantVillage dataset was used to evaluate the performance of the DL models. Although this dataset has a lot of images of several plant species with their diseases, it was taken in the lab. Therefore, it is expected to establish a large dataset of plant diseases in real conditions. Although some studies are using hyperspectral images of diseased leaves, and some DL frameworks are used for early detection of plant leaves diseases, problems that affect the widespread use of HSI in the early detection of plant diseases remain to be resolved. That is, for early plant disease detection, it is difﬁcult to obtain the labeled datasets, and even experienced experts cannot mark where the invisible disease symptoms are, and deﬁne purely invisible disease pixels, which is very important for HSI to detect plant disease. Plant disease detection is an important area of deep learning which has been addressed by many recent methods. However, there is a dire need to optimize these solutions for resource-constrained portable devices such as smartphones. This is a challenging problem because deep learning models are resource extensive in nature. This paper proposes an efﬁcient method to systematically classify plant disease symptoms using convolutional neural networks. These networks are memory efﬁcient and when coupled with the proposed training conﬁguration it enables rapid development of industrial applications by reducing the training times. These networks are memory efﬁcient and when coupled with the proposed training conﬁguration it enables rapid development of industrial applications by reducing the training times. Another critical problem arises with the improper distribution of samples among classes known as the class imbalance problem, which is addressed by employing a simple statistical methodology. Transfer learning is a known technique for training small datasets which transfers pre-trained weights learned on a large dataset. However, during transfer learning, negative transfer learning is a common problem. Therefore, a stepwise transfer learning approach is proposed which can help in fast convergence, while reducing overﬁtting and preventing negative transfer learning during knowledge transfer across domains. The system is trained and evaluated on two plant disease datasets i.e., PlantVillage (a publicly available dataset) and pepper disease dataset provided by the National Institute of Horticultural and Herbal Science, Republic of Korea. The pepper dataset is particularly challenging as it contains images from different parts of the plant such as the leaf, pulp, and stem. The proposed system has dominated the previous works on the PlantVillage dataset and achieved 99% and 99.69% accuracy on the Pepper dataset and PlantVillage datasets, respectively. [30] proposed the Freezeout method, where they progressively freeze the layers once a layer’s learning rate has reached zero. In this study, a similar approach is proposed, however, the intuition behind both methodologies is contrasting. In contrast, we propose an automatic algorithmic technique (stepwise transfer learning) which is a very different approach as compared to freezeout as it unfreezes the layers once the loss saturates for a speciﬁc number of epochs. This basic discrepancy between laboratory behavior and deployment fact is what encourages this extensive critique review. The fundamental conclusion of the literature review is clear: the lab-to-field performance gap is not the issue raised by architecture mostly but an issue of data, an issue of evaluation, or an issue of deployment prioritization. The evidence that is critically synthesized in this review includes convolutional neural network (CNN) architectures, transfer learning strategies, lightweight models, ensemble techniques, foundation model preprocessing, and explainability models. On critical analysis, it has been shown that dataset bias exposure, namely, the systematic usage of deliberated singleleaf laboratory images as both training and evaluation in the training, is the major cause of inflated accuracy reports. The high laboratory accuracy models are often presented by explainability models to focus on the background artifacts, as opposed to actual disease lesions, revealing a new weakness in the explainability models that cannot be identified by accuracy metrics. CNN-Based Classification The literature of plant disease detection is based on standard CNN architectures [32]. VGG16 [15] uses deep stacked convolutions with 98.5% accuracy at PlantVillage, but has 138M parameters, which is effectively impossible to run on rural smartphones. Importantly, despite being most capable of meeting laboratory standards, the VGG-class models have one of the widest lab-to-field accuracy gaps (17.5 percentage points), which implies that their large number of parameters allow them to memorize the artifacts of the dataset but not to learn the authentic aspects of the disease. E. Explainability-Integrated Methods There are only two studies among reviewed that include XAI validation, which are Nigar et al. [10] and Oad et al. [11]. And both found that, with Grad-CAM [21] and LIME [22], the high-accuracy models—97.8% and 99.3% respectively— did not focus on a disease lesion but fixed themselves at background areas or a leaf border. This is a very worrying discovery, supported by previous research on visualization of symptoms [35]: those models which are regularly released as being at high accuracy are not, in reality, identifying disease. They are identifying dataset-specific artifacts which are associated with disease labels in laboratory images but are absent in field images. The fact that the XAI validation has not been done much in the wider literature almost definitely means that the reality of the prevalence of this type of failure mode has been underestimated. This indicates that explainability validation should be enrolled in the next-generation models as one of the required verifications, and not a presented visualization facility, without which no deployment assertion can be regarded as trustworthy. SAM-Based Preprocessing for Distribution Gap Reduction Strict structural difference between laboratory and field data are that the laboratory datasets have a single leaf/image whereas the field images have numerous overlapping leaves. Moupojou et al. [12] proposed using the Segment Anything Model (SAM) [20] as a preprocessing step: SAM segments individual leaf instances, a discriminator filters non-leaf objects, and the least-anomalous leaf is passed to a CNN classifier. This pipeline yields 10–15% field accuracy improvements over direct whole-image classification, rehabilitating existing laboratory-trained models without retraining. As shown in Fig. 2, the pipeline bridges the structural mismatch between single-leaf training data and multi-leaf field inference. However, a critical limitation is that SAM introduces substantial preprocessing latency, making it unsuitable for realtime on-device deployment on entry-level smartphones—the primary target hardware for rural agricultural applications. VIII. RESEARCH GAPS IN EXISTING LITERATURE The critical synthesis presented in this review reveals four persistent and consequential gaps. Gap 1 — Systematic over-reliance on controlled datasets. The majority of published plant disease detection studies evaluate exclusively on PlantVillage or similar laboratory datasets. Independent cross-dataset evaluations consistently show 10–15 percentage point accuracy inflation under controlled conditions [7], [8], [33]. Yet the research community continues to publish and cite laboratory-only results as evidence of deployment readiness. This constitutes a systemic evaluation failure: models are not being tested in conditions resembling those where they will be used. Gap 2 — Absence of standardized field evaluation protocols. No community-wide standard exists for distribution shift evaluation. Studies use incompatible class counts (10 to 38), metric definitions (weighted vs. macro-averaged accuracy), augmentation pipelines, and hardware specifications [9]. This heterogeneity makes cross-study comparison unreliable and allows evaluation practices that systematically inflate reported performance to persist unchallenged. A standardized benchmark with fixed field-evaluation protocol—analogous to ImageNet for general vision—is a critical missing infrastructure for this domain [25]. Gap 3 — Limited deployment-focused architecture research. The vast majority of architecture papers optimize for laboratory accuracy as their sole metric. Only 2 of the 13 studies reviewed in Table II incorporated XAI validation, and both revealed spurious correlation learning despite high reported accuracy [10], [11]. The research community currently has no mechanism for distinguishing models that have genuinely learned disease features from models that have learned to recognize controlled-environment artifacts. Until XAI validation becomes a standard publication requirement, accuracy numbers cannot be trusted as evidence of genuine disease recognition. IX. Model compression techniques—quantization, pruning, and knowledge distillation—can reduce model size by 4–8× with minimal accuracy loss, enabling deployment on entry-level smartphones without GPU hardware [18]. Federated learning [23] enables collaborative training across geographically distributed farms without pooling raw image data, addressing data privacy constraints and the connectivity limitations of rural areas. Initial applications to agricultural imaging show promise for learning robust representations from heterogeneous field conditions. Field-realistic dataset construction remains the highestpriority infrastructure need [33]. The research community requires diverse multi-geography, multi-season, multi-crop field datasets with pathologist-verified annotations at a scale substantially exceeding FieldPlant’s 5,170 images. Without such datasets, the lab-to-field gap cannot be systematically closed regardless of architectural innovation. Multi-modal fusion combining leaf imagery with complementary data—weather records, soil composition, historical disease incidence maps—can improve early-stage infection diagnosis where visual symptoms are not yet distinguishable from image data alone [26]. CONCLUSION This review has critically examined deep learning-based plant disease detection with a focus on the persistent and consequential gap between laboratory benchmark performance and real-world field deployment. The synthesis of evidence from existing literature supports four principal conclusions. First, the deployment bottleneck is not architectural—it is a data problem, an evaluation problem, and ultimately a deployment prioritization problem. ABSTRACT Global plant diseases represent a major threat to agriculture and represent significant economic losses constituting an important threat to food security. This study introduces a transformative hybrid framework for plant disease diagnosis and severity estimation, combining the strengths of advanced deep learning architectures: Detection Transformer (DETR), Swin Transformer and SAM2-UNet. The proposed methodology incorporates classification, detection, segmentation, and severity estimation in the form of a unified pipeline to address the complexities of real-world agricultural settings, including variable lighting, background variety and large-scale fields. With a hierarchical attention mechanism for efficient feature extraction, the Swin Transformer achieves a top 1 accuracy of 85.6%, and a top 5 accuracy of 96.2%. Utilizing its encoder-decoder attention technique, Detection Transformer (DETR) effectively detects diseases by employing an encoder to forecast bounding boxes and class labels for affected areas. Segmentation performance is enhanced with SAM2-UNet, achieving a pixel-level segmentation with a Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC) of 94.7%, cleanly delineating disease-affected areas. DATA SCARCITY CHALLENGES AND MITIGATION STRATEGIES Data scarcity continues to be a major obstacle in diagnosing plant diseases, primarily in three dimensions that our framework tackles directly. First, the long-tail distribution of disease samples (Plantseg has 9 cash crop diseases and 45 vegetable diseases) is creating classification bottlenecks where rare classes in baseline models can drop 12-15% in accuracy compared to common ones [20], [27]. Second, pixel-level annotations have incredible annotation demands in terms of time for severity estimation, an average of 38.7 minutes/image for pixels vs. 6.2 minutes/image for just bounding boxes [31], which is quite limiting when it comes to real-world applications. Third, domain shifts lead to performance declines (<22.4% using typical CNN) when comparing images taken in a lab (PlantVillage has 54,309 studio-captured samples) vs. actual ones in the field (our PlantSeg has 11,458 custom images taken) [21]. Simply put, our framework builds ways to counter these issues with (1) Swin Transformer using shifted window attention methodology, achieving 85.6% top-1 accuracy on rare classes (compared to only 72.3% for ResNet50 [32]), (2) Detection Transformer (DETR) set prediction approach resulting in 41% less propagation in annotation errors versus cascade RCNN [33], and (3) SAM2-UNet, which has shown to have the ability to use transfer learning with 60% fewer labeled samples (and still had 94.7% DSC)

These diseases can greatly impact yield and productivity, making early and accurate detection vital, especially in staple crops like potatoes. Traditional manual methods, as well as some existing machine learning and deep learning techniques, often lack accuracy and generalizability due to factors such as variability in real-world conditions. This study proposes a novel approach to improve potato plant disease detection and identification using a hybrid deep-learning model, EfficientNetV2B3+ViT. This model combines the strengths of a Convolutional Neural Network - EfficientNetV2B3 and a Vision Transformer (ViT). Traditional methods for disease diagnosis heavily rely on human observation and manual tests, which are prone to errors and inconsistencies. Moreover, they can be time-consuming and impractical for large-scale operations [9–11]. The potential for human error is high given the complex nature of plant diseases and hardly distinguishable differences in their symptoms. For example, early blight and late blight, though caused by different pathogens, present similar symptoms in their early stages, making them difficult to distinguish without expert knowledge or laboratory testing [5, 12]. Each patch is then linearly transformed into a one-dimensional vector by flattening and multiplying by a learnable matrix. This sequence of vectors is subsequently fed into a standard transformer encoder. The transformer encoder captures the global context of the image by modeling long-range dependencies between these patches. This is facilitated by the selfattention mechanism of the transformer, which enables each patch to attend to all other patches in a weighted manner. The weights are determined by the similarity between patches, allowing the model to emphasize the most relevant parts of the image. The output of the transformer encoder is a sequence of vectors, each representing a patch of the image enriched with contextual information from all other patches. The vector corresponding to the first patch, or a special “classification” token added to the sequence, is then processed through a linear layer to yield the final classification output. Conclusion The study demonstrates the potential of the EfficientNetV2B3+ViT hybrid model for improving the accuracy of potato plant disease detection and identification. The proposed model achieved an accuracy of 85.06% on a diverse dataset that reflects real-world agricultural conditions, outperforming the individual CNN and ViT models. However, the model performance varied across different disease classes, with the ‘Pest’ class posing particular challenges due to potential feature overlap with the ‘Fungi’ class. Further testing on additional datasets and crops is necessary to establish the broader applicability and generalizability of the proposed approach. Future research should focus on refining the model architecture, incorporating explainable AI techniques to provide insight into the decision-making process, and investigating the transferability of the approach to other crops and diseases. Conventional disease detection techniques that depend on the farmer's experience or professional advice, are frequently sluggish, arbitrary, and prone to mistakes. text: Precision agriculture in the age of AI: A systematic review of machine learning methods for crop disease detection Munir Majdalawieh a , Carla Martins b, Mohammed Radi c, Maher Alaraj a,* , Shafaq Khan d a Department of Information Systems and Technology Management, College of Technological Innovation, Zayed University, Dubai 19282, United Arab Emirates b ULS de Sao Joao, Alameda Professor Hernani Monteiro, 4200-319 Porto, Portugal c Department of Electronic and Electrical Engineering, College of Engineering, Design and Physical Sciences, Brunel University of London, Uxbridge UB8 3PH, UK d School of Computer Science, University of Windsor, Ontario N9B 3P4, Canada A R T I C L E I N F O Keywords: Computer vision Crop disease detection Deep learning Machine learning Precision agriculture Plant pathology A B S T R A C T Artificial Intelligence (AI) has become a critical tool in modern precision agriculture, particularly in the detection of plant diseases and pests. However, some studies have explored the use of high-precision imaging techniques, such as hyperspectral and multispectral imaging, which provide richer spectral information but come at a higher cost due to the need for specialised cameras and sensors. Even so, studies that utilised high-precision images do not neces sarily achieve higher accuracy than those relying on RGB images. The average accuracy for RGB-based models was 96.94 %, whereas models using hyperspectral and multispectral imaging achieved an average accuracy of 95.81 %. High-precision imaging techniques require significantly greater computational resources as they generate large, high-dimensional datasets that necessitate advanced processing tech niques and higher memory capacity. Additionally, these methods often require specific environmental conditions for capturing optimal spectral data, which can limit their real-world applicability. This makes RGB images the preferred choice for large-scale, real-world applications where cost-effectiveness, scalability, and ease of deployment are prior itized over maximum accuracy. The first gap concerns geographical bias, as there is a disproportionate concentration of data bases originating from the Asian continent compared to other regions. This imbalance may lead to artificial intelligence models with limited generalizability to other areas with different cultural, climatic, and pest/ disease pressures. Given this geographic imbalance, there is a clear need for more diverse and representative datasets from underrepresented regions, such as Africa, Europe, and South America. Expanding dataset diversity will improve the robustness, adaptability, and generalisability of AI-based plant disease detection models, ensuring that the method ologies developed can be effectively applied across different climates, crop types, and agricultural conditions. Conclusion Currently, deep-learning models, particularly CNNs and ViTs, deliver the most accurate results for detecting crop diseases. Further progress depends on creating diverse, well-labelled datasets and building light weight systems that work in low-resource farm settings. Closing geographic data gaps and adopting common annotation standards are key to turning research success into real-world impact. Future studies should prioritize the development of hybrid AI models that combine the efficiency of classical machine learning with the accuracy of deep learning, aiming to balance performance with computational demands. Greater attention must also be given to the creation of open, multiregional datasets that capture a wide diversity of crops, disease types, and environmental conditions to enhance model generalizability. Object detection technology is one of the hot spots in current research. It has been developed to overcome the limitations of conventional methods of disease diagnosis. It is optimized by combining best practices and techniques from previous versions of YOLO and incorporating new ideas and innovations. Key features that distinguish YOLOv8 from other object detection algorithms include its efficient and powerful network architecture, its use of deep learning techniques, and its ability to handle large data sets. It is also designed to have a small memory footprint and high computational efficiency, making it suitable for real-time object detection tasks even on low-end hardware. This work aims to demonstrate the effectiveness of enhanced YOLOv8 for crop disease detection on the challenging PlantDoc dataset, which includes real-world images of various crops affected by different diseases, captured in scenarios with complex backgrounds and lighting conditions. This systematic review analyzes deep learning approaches for plant disease detection using RGB and hyperspectral imaging, examining their evolution from classical image processing to modern neural architectures. We evaluate state-of-the-art models across 11 benchmark datasets, revealing significant performance gaps between laboratory conditions (95–99% accuracy) and field deployment (70–85% accuracy). Transformerbased architectures demonstrate superior robustness, with SWIN achieving 88% accuracy on real-world datasets compared to 53% for traditional CNNs. Our analysis identifies three critical deployment constraints: environmental variability sensitivity, economic barriers (500–2000 USD for RGB vs. 20,000–50,000 USD for hyperspectral systems), and interpretability requirements for farmer adoption. Case studies of successful platforms (Plantix with 10+ million users) highlight the importance of offline functionality and multilingual support.

Challenges in automated plant disease detection Automating plant disease detection requires a system atic and technology-driven approach. Addressing the challenges involved is crucial for successfully integrating advanced detection systems into agriculture. This section outlines key issues and breaks them down into sub-sec tions for clarity. Diversity across plant species Plant species diversity presents significant challenges for deep learning-based disease detection systems. Each species displays unique morphological and physiologi cal characteristics, requiring specialized training data for accurate identification. A model trained on tomato leaves, for example, often struggles to identify diseases in cucumber plants due to fundamental differences in leaf structure and coloration patterns. This challenge extends to the problem of catastrophic forgetting, where models retrained on new species lose accuracy on previ ously learned plants.

This challenge extends to the problem of catastrophic forgetting, where models retrained on new species lose accuracy on previ ously learned plants. Despite ongoing research efforts to address these transferability limitations [15, 98], develop ing robust cross-species models remains a critical chal lenge for widespread agricultural application. Variability in image datasets Real-world agricultural environments introduce sub stantial variability that complicates consistent disease detection. Factors such as illumination conditions (bright sunlight versus cloudy days), background complexity (soil types, mulch, neighboring plants), viewing angles, and growth stages significantly impact image characteristics. Models must demonstrate resilience to these variations to ensure reliable performance across diverse field con ditions [30]. Additionally, seasonal changes affect leaf appearance and disease manifestation, further compli cating the development of year-round detection systems. Techniques such as domain adaptation and robust fea ture extraction are essential to overcome these environ mental variability challenges. Constraints of annotated datasets The development of accurate plant disease detec tion models relies heavily on well-annotated datasets, which remain difficult to obtain at scale. Expert plant pathologists must verify disease classifications, mak ing high-quality dataset creation resource-intensive and time-consuming. This expert dependency creates bottle necks in dataset expansion and diversification. Further more, the specialized knowledge required for accurate annotation means datasets often contain regional biases or coverage gaps for certain species and disease variants.

Imbalances in class distribution Natural imbalances in disease occurrence create signifi cant challenges for developing equitable disease detec tion systems. Common diseases typically have abundant examples, while rare conditions suffer from limited rep resentation in training datasets. This imbalance often biases models toward frequently occurring diseases at the expense of accurately identifying rare but potentially devastating conditions. Recent research has explored techniques such as weighted loss functions, data aug mentation, and specialized sampling methods to address these distribution issues [16, 214, 240]. Despite these advances, ensuring balanced performance across all disease categories remains an ongoing challenge, par ticularly for emerging or geographically limited plant pathogens. Challenges in early detection Identifying plant diseases during their initial develop ment stages offers the greatest intervention potential but presents substantial technical difficulties. Early infec tion symptoms often manifest as minute physiologi cal changes before visible symptoms appear, requiring highly sensitive detection capabilities. These early indi cators may include minor spectral shifts, slight texture alterations, or minimal color variations that conven tional imaging systems frequently miss [164]. Addition ally, distinguishing between early disease symptoms and other plant stressors (nutrient deficiencies, water stress, or mechanical damage) requires sophisticated discrimi nation algorithms. Improving early detection sensitiv ity while maintaining specificity represents a critical research direction for minimizing crop losses and reduc ing preventative chemical applications. Deployment challenges in resource-limited areas Implementing advanced disease detection technolo gies in resource-constrained agricultural regions intro duces unique adoption barriers. Rural areas frequently lack reliable internet connectivity, stable power sup plies, and technical support infrastructure necessary for cloud-based systems. Practical solutions must balance technological sophistication with local constraints, pri oritizing user-friendly interfaces and offline functional ity. Context-specific customization focusing on regionally prevalent crops and diseases proves more valuable than generic systems.

Plant diseases: biological context for detection methods Understanding the biological basis of plant diseases is crucial for developing effective detection technologies. Plant diseases are defined as harmful physiological pro cesses caused by persistent irritation from pathogens or environmental factors [186]. These diseases exhibit distinct biological signatures that modern imaging tech niques can capture at different stages of development. The primary disease agents create detectable patterns that inform detection system design. Role of artificial intelligence in plant disease detection Artificial Intelligence (AI), particularly through machine and deep learning, has emerged as a transformative force in plant disease detection. These technologies analyze complex visual patterns in plant imagery to identify dis eases with unprecedented speed and accuracy compared to traditional manual inspection methods. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have been particularly effective, with reviews demonstrating their high accuracy in clas sifying various leaf diseases such as blight and powdery mildew. The practical implementation of these technolo gies has extended to field-deployable solutions. Mobile applications like Plantix [199] use image recognition to identify over 60 different plant diseases and provide treat ment recommendations, while UAV-mounted systems conduct aerial surveillance to detect disease hotspots across large cultivation areas [210]. These applications demonstrate how AI bridges the gap between advanced algorithms and practical agricultural needs. This tech nological context provides the foundation for our sub sequent analysis of detection methodologies, beginning with an examination of the datasets and evaluation met rics that underpin both RGB and hyperspectral imaging approaches to plant disease identification. YOLO is a single-stage target detection model proposed by Joseph Redmon et al. in 2015. Traditional target detection frameworks, such as R-CNN, typically involve a multistage process that includes candidate region generation, feature extraction, and bracket box regression. While such processes can significantly improve accuracy, real-time execution is often not feasible due to their inherent limitations, hence the term multistage target detection algorithms. In contrast, single-stage target detection algorithms can omit the candidate region generation step and significantly improve model training speed while maintaining higher accuracy. Therefore, more and more researchers are focusing on single-stage target detection algorithms. Currently, among various single-stage target detection algorithms, the YOLO algorithm has the best comprehensive performance and has been widely used in the industry. text: Delving deeper into the RPN's mechanism, one discerns its bifurcation into two primary facets. On the classification front, it evaluates anchor boxes, discerning whether a given region truly encapsulates an object, thereby distinguishing between positive and negative anchors. In terms of regression, it computes the offset between the anchor boxes and the true object boundaries, achieving more refined object localization. This harmonious amalgamation of both mechanisms ensures that RPN generates high-quality object candidate regions for subsequent processing. After the RPN generates candidate regions based on predicted outputs, it further employs the positive anchor boxes and their corresponding offset data to shape proposal boxes. To ensure these proposal boxes are of high quality and redundant ones are minimized, RPN utilizes an Intersection-over-Union (IoU) threshold for screening. Subsequently, the entire network employs an ROI pooling layer, constructing a fixed-size feature map for every refined candidate region, laying the groundwork for upcoming classification and boundary regression tasks. text: Within RCNN, the extraction of ROI is typically contingent on selective search. Furthermore, it's noteworthy that the ROI doesn't need to flawlessly encapsulate an object; a general inclusion suffices as subsequent procedures will fine-tune its positioning. Within Fast R-CNN, ROI Projection is a technique mapping ROIs from the original image onto the CNN feature map. The source image first undergoes CNN processing to yield a feature map. Leveraging this feature map, the feature region corresponding to the original ROI can be discerned. This modus operandi permits operations not directly on the source image but on its correlated feature map. Mapping each pixel of the original image back to the feature map captures a more expansive context by harnessing the pixels' receptive fields. ROI Pooling is a normalization procedure converting varying sized ROIs into uniform feature maps to be compatible with subsequent neural network processing. Specifically, given a predetermined output size, ROI Pooling segments the ROI into numerous smaller regions, executing Max Pooling over these, ensuring each retains only its maximum value. This ensures a consistently sized output feature map irrespective of the original ROI's dimensions. In intricate scenarios, ROI Pooling may employ diverse spatial block partitioning strategies, for instance, concurrently segmenting an ROI into 4x4, 2x2, and 1x1 spatial blocks, concatenating the pooling results of these blocks to generate a lengthier feature vector. text: III. CROP DISEASE AND PEST DIAGNOSIS TECHNIQUES A. PlantDoc dataset Due to plant diseases, India incurs approximately 35% crop yield losses annually. Computer vision technologies have emerged as potential solutions to the intelligent detection challenge of these diseases. Nevertheless, the paucity of disease datasets available for real-world applications renders the task challenging. Addressing this need, Singh et al.[5] introduced the PlantDoc dataset in 2019. Focused on collecting images of plant diseases in realworld scenarios, the PlantDoc dataset effectively mirrors realworld plant disease conditions. The dataset encompasses 13 plant species, 27 disease categories, and a total of 2,598 images. For precise model training and testing, all images were annotated with bounding boxes using the LabelImg tool, yielding 9,216 bounding boxes for model training. Deformable Convolution Networks Traditional convolution operations employ fixed spatial sampling locations on images. Although multi-layer stacking can capture spatial variations within a certain range, this approach remains limited when addressing intricate spatial deformations. To address this limitation, Dai et al. introduced deformable convolution. This technique enhances the spatial sampling capacity of convolution operations by introducing offsets for each sampling point within the convolution kernel. This means that convolution no longer samples at fixed spatial grid points but can sample at any location, thus better capturing deformation information within the image.[6][7] Figure 7 illustrates deformable convolution. Fig. 7. Deformable Convolution Illustration Deformable convolution enhances the spatial sampling capability of traditional convolution by predicting offsets for each sampling point and employs bilinear interpolation to acquire the corresponding feature values. This mechanism bestows the model with superior spatial modeling capabilities, allowing it to autonomously capture intricate and non-fixed spatial deformations in images, eliminating the need for manually designed specific sampling patterns. When Deformable Convolutional Networks are integrated with Faster R-CNN, the model can more efficiently learn and discern different morphologies, postures, and scales of crop disease characteristics. In the diagnosis of crop pests and diseases, this suggests that the model can more precisely detect and differentiate diseases with irregular morphologies and postures, such as curled, spotted, or irregular leaves. Moreover, the model adeptly handles complex backgrounds, light variations, and obstructions, thus offering users more accurate diagnostic results in practical applications.

text: ResNet18-Based Intelligent System for Automated Potato Leaf Disease Detection and Classification Pratham Kaushik Centre for Research Impact & Outcome, Chitkara University Institute of Engineering and Technology Chitkara University, Rajpura-140401, Punjab, India pratham.kaushik@chitkara.edu.in Pooja Sharma Chitkara Centre for Research and Development, Chitkara University, Himachal Pradesh-174103 India pooja.sharma.orp@chitkara.edu.in Abstract--- This study leverages the ResNet18 deep learning model to classify potato leaves into three categories: Healthy, Early Blight, and Late Blight. Image dataset of high resolution was used in the study and the images were pre-processed by resizing, normalizing and by applying data augmentation to improve the predictive power of the model. To overcome this, the given data was divided into training, validation, and test datasets to maintain equal class distributions and to check the efficiency of the proposed approach. The ResNet18 model yielded an overall accuracy of 88%, with the precision, recall, and F1-scores being relatively even across all classes. Evaluation of confusion matrix and classification report brought about appreciation of the models’ performance, with only minor misclassifications mostly between similar diseases. This study demonstrates that ResNet18 is suitable for automated disease identification to enhance the management of diseases in farming. The future work involves collecting a larger and more diverse dataset, investigating the possibilities of utilizing advanced ensemble learning approaches and implementing the applications in real-world scenarios. text: B. Research Opportunities As the field of plant disease detection evolves, several research opportunities are emerging in both model improvements and application scenarios. These opportunities aim to refine detection capabilities, improve scalability, and make plant disease detection systems more practical and effective in real-world settings. 1) Model Improvements Few-shot Learning: Few-shot learning enables models to learn from limited labeled examples[24], which is valuable in plant disease detection[26],[35], where data for certain diseases is scarce or imbalanced. This approach improves model generalization[23], enhancing performance in recognizing rare or underrepresented diseases. Self-supervised Learning: Self-supervised learning enables models to use large amounts of unlabeled data, generating useful representations from the data itself. This reduces reliance on manually labeled data, making it a promising approach for enhancing plant disease detection, particularly when annotated data is scarce or hard to obtain[30],[37].
